source_text: Καίτοι καὶ εἰ ἄφωνος ἔστη μετὰ τὴν τῆς γλώττης ἐκκοπὴν ὁ μάρτυς, καὶ οὕτως αὐτῷ τὰ τῶν ἀγώνων πεπλήρωτο, καὶ ὁ στέφανος ἀπήρτιστο· ἧττα γὰρ μεγίστη καὶ σαφὴς ἀπόδειξις ἦν τὸ τὴν γλῶτταν τεμεῖν. Εἰ γὰρ μὴ ἐφοβοῦ τὴν γλῶτταν, ὦ μιαρὲ καὶ παμμίαρε, τίνος ἕνεκεν αὐτὴν ἀπέτεμες; τίνος ἕνεκεν οὐκ ἀφῆκας τῶν παλαισμάτων τὴν ὑπόθεσιν, ἀλλ' ἀπέκλεισας τὸ στάδιον; Ὥσπερ ἂν εἴ τις παγκρατιάζειν μέλλων, εἶτα πληγὰς ἀφάτους λαβὼν, καὶ μὴ δυνάμενος ἀντιστῆναι λοιπὸν, κελεύσειεν ἐκκοπῆναι τοῦ ἀνταγωνιστοῦ τὰς χεῖρας, καὶ οὕτως αὐτὸν παίοι, οὐ χρεία λοιπὸν ἑτέρας ἀποδείξεως πρὸς τὸ τὴν νίκην τῷ τὰς χεῖρας ἐκκοπέντι ψηφίσασθαι· οὕτω δὴ καὶ ἐπὶ τοῦ μάρτυρος σαφεστέρα πάντων ἀπόδειξις ἡ τῆς γλώττης ἐκκοπὴ γέγονε τῆς κατὰ τοῦ διαβόλου νίκης. Εἰ γὰρ καὶ θνητὴ ἦν ἡ γλῶττα, ἀλλ' ἐπειδὴ ἀθάνατα τραύματα δέδωκε τῷ διαβόλῳ, διὰ τοῦτο κατ' ἐκείνης ἔπνευσεν ὅλος, ἑαυτὸν μὲν εἰς μείζονα καθιστῶν αἰσχύνην, τῷ δὲ μάρτυρι λαμπρότερον ποιῶν τὸν στέφανον. Ὥσπερ γὰρ θαυμαστὸν χωρὶς ῥίζης δένδρον ἰδεῖν, καὶ χωρὶς πηγῆς ποταμόν· οὕτω καὶ χωρὶς γλώττης φωνήν. δʹ. Ποῦ νῦν εἰσιν οἱ τῇ τῶν σωμάτων ἀναστάσει διαπιστοῦντες; Ἰδοὺ ἡ φωνὴ καὶ ἀπέθανε καὶ ἀνέστη, καὶ ἐν μιᾷ καιροῦ ῥοπῇ ταῦτα ἀμφότερα γέγονε. Καίτοι τοῦτο τῆς τῶν σωμάτων ἀναστάσεως πολλῷ μεῖζόν ἐστιν· ἐκεῖ μὲν γὰρ ἡ φύσις τῶν σωμάτων ὑπόκειται, ἡ σύνθεσις δὲ διαλέλυται μόνον· ἐνταῦθα δὲ αὐτὴ ἡ ὑπόθεσις τῆς φωνῆς ἀνῄρητο, ἀλλ' ὅμως λαμπροτέρα πάλιν ἐγίγνετο. Καίτοι γε αὐλοῦ τὰς γλωττίδας ἂν ἀφέλῃς, ἄχρηστον λοιπὸν κεῖται τὸ ὄργανον· ἀλλ' οὐχ οὕτως ὁ αὐλὸς ὁ πνευματικὸς, ἀλλὰ καὶ τὴν γλῶτταν ἀφαιρεθεὶς οὐ μόνον οὐκ ἦν ἄφωνος, ἀλλὰ καὶ ἐμμελέστερον καὶ μυστικώτερον ἠφίει μέλος, καὶ μετὰ πλείονος τῆς ἐκπλήξεως. Καὶ ἐπὶ κιθάρας δὲ πάλιν, ἂν τὸ πλῆκτρόν τις ἐξαρπάσῃ μόνον, ἀργὸς ὁ τεχνίτης, ἄχρηστος ἡ τέχνη, μάταιον τὸ ὄργανον γίγνεται· ἐνταῦθα δὲ οὐδὲν τοιοῦτον, ἀλλὰ τοὐναντίον ἅπαν. Καὶ γὰρ ἦν κιθάρα τὸ στόμα, ἦν πλῆκτρον ἡ γλῶττα, τεχνίτης δὲ ἡ ψυχὴ, καὶ τέχνη ἡ ὁμολογία· ἀλλ' ὅμως ἀφαιρεθέντος τοῦ πλήκτρου, τῆς γλώσσης λέγω, οὔτε ὁ τεχνίτης, οὔτε ἡ τέχνη, οὔτε τὸ ὄργανον ἄχρηστον γέγονεν, ἀλλὰ πάντα τὴν οἰκείαν δύναμιν ἐπεδείκνυτο. Τίς ταῦτα ἐποίησε; τίς ταῦτα ἐπέδειξε τὰ θαυμαστὰ καὶ παράδοξα; Ὁ Θεὸς ὁ ποιῶν θαυμάσια μόνος, περὶ οὗ φησιν ὁ Δαυῒδ, Κύριε ὁ Κύριος ἡμῶν, ὡς θαυμαστὸν τὸ ὄνομά σου ἐν πάσῃ τῇ γῇ· ὅτι ἐπήρθη ἡ μεγαλοπρέπειά σου ὑπεράνω τῶν οὐρανῶν· ἐκ στόματος νηπίων καὶ θηλαζόντων κατηρτίσω αἶνον. Τότε μὲν οὖν ἐκ στόματος νηπίων καὶ θηλαζόντων, νῦν δὲ ἐκ στόματος ἀγλώτ των· τότε φύσις ἄωρος; νῦν δὲ στόμα ἔρημον· ἁπαλὴ τότε ἡ ῥίζα ἐπὶ τῶν παίδων ἦν, ἀλλ' ὁ καρπὸς ἀπηρτισμένος· ἐνταῦθα δὲ καὶ αὐτὴ ἡ ῥίζα ἀνῄρητο, καὶ ἡ τοῦ καρποῦ γένεσις οὐκ ἐκωλύετο· καρπὸς γὰρ γλώττης φωνή. Θαυμαστότερα τὰ ὕστερα τῶν προτέρων. Καὶ γὰρ ἵνα ταῦτα μὴ ἀπιστῆται, διὰ τοῦτο ἐκεῖνα προέδραμεν, ἵνα ἐν τούτοις μὴ θορυβώμεθα, τῆς διανοίας ἡμῶν ἐν ἐκείνοις προεθισθείσης Διὰ τοῦτο, ταῦτα ἀπήντησεν, ἵνα ἐκεῖνα τὰ ἀφανῆ καὶ τὰ παλαιὰ ἀπὸ τῶν φανερῶν καὶ νεωστὶ γενομένων πιστεύηται.
thought_title: The tongue's removal proves the martyr's victory
orientation: Chrysostom is arguing that even if Romanus had been silenced after his tongue was cut out, the very removal of the tongue would itself prove the devil's defeat, and he now presses this point with a series of comparisons.
pass_a_gloss: And yet even if the martyr stood voiceless after the cutting out of the tongue, even so the things of the contests had been fulfilled for him, and the crown had been completed; for the cutting of the tongue was a very great and clear proof. For if you did not fear the tongue, O defiled and utterly defiled one, for the sake of what did you cut it out? For the sake of what did you not leave the subject of the wrestling, but shut up the stadium? Just as if someone about to fight in the pancration, then receiving unutterable blows, and no longer able to resist, should order the hands of the opponent to be cut off, and should thus strike him, there is no longer need of another proof for the victory to be voted to the one whose hands were cut off; so indeed also in the case of the martyr the cutting out of the tongue became a proof clearer than all of the victory over the devil. For even if the tongue was mortal, yet since it gave immortal wounds to the devil, for this reason he breathed wholly against it, placing himself into greater shame, and making the crown more splendid for the martyr. For just as it is wonderful to see a tree without a root, and a river without a spring; so also a voice without a tongue. 4. Where now are those who disbelieve in the resurrection of bodies? Behold the voice both died and rose, and in one moment of time both these things happened. And yet this is much greater than the resurrection of bodies; for there the nature of bodies lies beneath, and only the composition has been dissolved; but here the very foundation of the voice had been destroyed, but nevertheless it became more splendid again. And yet if you take away the reeds of a flute, the instrument lies useless thereafter; but not so the spiritual flute, but even when deprived of the tongue it was not only not voiceless, but also it sent forth a more harmonious and more mystical melody, and with more amazement. And again in the case of a lyre, if someone snatches away only the plectrum, the craftsman is idle, the craft is useless, the instrument becomes vain; but here nothing of this sort, but the opposite in every way. For the mouth was a lyre, the tongue was a plectrum, the soul was the craftsman, and the craft was the confession; but nevertheless when the plectrum was removed, I mean the tongue, neither the craftsman, nor the craft, nor the instrument became useless, but all displayed their own power. Who made these things? Who displayed these wonderful and paradoxical things? God who alone does wonders, about whom David says, Lord our Lord, how wonderful is your name in all the earth; because your majesty was lifted up above the heavens; out of the mouth of infants and nursing babies you prepared praise. Then indeed out of the mouth of infants and nursing babies, but now out of the mouth of the tongueless; then an unripe nature; now a desolate mouth; then the root was tender in the case of the children, but the fruit was complete; but here the root itself had been destroyed, and the production of the fruit was not hindered; for the fruit of the tongue is voice. The later things are more wonderful than the former. For in order that these things might not be disbelieved, for this reason those things ran ahead, in order that in these things we might not be troubled, our mind having been accustomed beforehand in those things. For this reason these things happened, in order that those unseen and ancient things might be believed from the visible and recently occurring things.

choices.term: ἧττα γὰρ μεγίστη καὶ σαφὴς ἀπόδειξις ἦν τὸ τὴν γλῶτταν τεμεῖν
choices.english: for the cutting of the tongue was a very great and clear proof
choices.why: ἧττα is a textual problem; the sense requires 'defeat' or 'proof' of the devil's defeat, and the following sentence confirms the proof reading
rejected: for the defeat was a very great and clear proof

choices.term: τίνος ἕνεκεν οὐκ ἀφῆκας τῶν παλαισμάτων τὴν ὑπόθεσιν, ἀλλ' ἀπέκλεισας τὸ στάδιον
choices.english: for the sake of what did you not leave the subject of the wrestling, but shut up the stadium
choices.why: ὑπόθεσις here means the ground or occasion of the contest, and στάδιον the arena; the athletic metaphor is sustained
rejected: why did you not leave the hypothesis of the struggles, but closed the stadium

choices.term: ἀλλ' ἐπειδὴ ἀθάνατα τραύματα δέδωκε τῷ διαβόλῳ
choices.english: yet since it gave immortal wounds to the devil
choices.why: The tongue's wounds to the devil are 'immortal' in the sense of lasting and irreparable, contrasting with the tongue's own mortality
rejected: but since it gave deathless wounds to the devil

choices.why: The metaphor of the mouth as a flute is explicit in the text; 'spiritual' marks the contrast with the physical instrument

choices.english: out of the mouth of the tongueless
choices.why: The text has a word break (ἀγλώτ των) likely due to line division; the sense is 'tongueless ones' referring to Romanus
rejected: out of the mouth of those without tongues

choices.term: τῆς διανοίας ἡμῶν ἐν ἐκείνοις προεθισθείσης
choices.english: our mind having been accustomed beforehand in those things
choices.why: The genitive absolute explains the purpose of the earlier wonders: to prepare the mind so that the later wonders would not disturb
rejected: our thought having been pre-accustomed in those things

pass_b_english: And yet even if the martyr had stood speechless after his tongue was cut out, his contests would still have been complete and his crown finished. For the cutting of the tongue was a very great and clear proof. If you did not fear the tongue, you foul and utterly defiled one, why did you cut it out? Why did you not leave the ground of the wrestling alone, but shut up the arena? It is as if someone about to fight in the pancration, after receiving unspeakable blows and no longer able to resist, should order his opponent's hands to be cut off and then strike him. No further proof would be needed to award the victory to the one whose hands were cut off. So too in the martyr's case, the cutting out of the tongue became the clearest proof of all of his victory over the devil. For even though the tongue was mortal, yet since it gave immortal wounds to the devil, he breathed against it with all his force, making himself more shameful and making the martyr's crown more brilliant. For just as it is wonderful to see a tree without a root and a river without a spring, so too a voice without a tongue.

Where now are those who disbelieve in the resurrection of bodies? Look: the voice both died and rose again, and both happened in a single moment. And yet this is far greater than the resurrection of bodies. For there the nature of bodies remains; only the composition is dissolved. But here the very ground of the voice was destroyed, and yet it became more brilliant again. If you remove the reeds of a flute, the instrument lies useless from then on. But not so the spiritual flute: even when the tongue was removed, it was not only not voiceless, but it sent forth a more melodious and more mystical song, and with greater astonishment. And again with a lyre: if someone merely snatches away the plectrum, the craftsman is idle, the craft useless, the instrument vain. But here nothing of the sort—rather the complete opposite. For the mouth was the lyre, the tongue was the plectrum, the soul was the craftsman, and the craft was confession. Yet when the plectrum was removed—I mean the tongue—neither the craftsman nor the craft nor the instrument became useless, but all displayed their proper power. Who did these things? Who displayed these wonderful and paradoxical things? God, who alone does wonders, about whom David says, "O Lord, our Lord, how wonderful is your name in all the earth! For your majesty is lifted high above the heavens. Out of the mouths of infants and nursing babies you have prepared praise" (Psalm 8:1-2). Then it was out of the mouths of infants and nursing babies; now it is out of the mouth of the tongueless. Then the nature was unripe; now the mouth is desolate. Then the root on the children was tender, but the fruit was complete. Here the root itself was destroyed, and yet the production of the fruit was not hindered—for the fruit of the tongue is voice. The later things are more wonderful than the former. For so that these things might not be disbelieved, those earlier things ran ahead, so that we might not be disturbed by these, our mind having been accustomed beforehand in those things. For this reason these things came to meet us, so that those unseen and ancient things might be believed from the visible things that had just happened.
notes: ἧττα in the first sentence is likely a corruption or unusual usage; the context demands a word meaning 'proof' or 'defeat' of the devil, and the following sentence (ἀπόδειξις) supports reading it as proof.
ἀγλώτ των appears to be split across a line break; the intended word is ἀγλώττων (tongueless).

last_rejected.why: ἔστη means 'stood' intransitively, but 'stood speechless' implies remaining; better 'had remained speechless' or 'had been left speechless'
last_rejected.fix: And yet even if the martyr had remained speechless after his tongue was cut out
last_rejected.ruling: ἔστη is aorist of ἵστημι; 'stood speechless' correctly conveys the aorist action. No meaning lost.

last_rejected.why: ὑπόθεσις here means 'subject matter' or 'theme' of contests, not 'ground'; 'leave the wrestling alone' misses 'let the contest's premise stand'
last_rejected.fix: Why did you not leave the wrestling-match's premise alone
last_rejected.ruling: ὑπόθεσις can mean 'ground/basis'; 'ground of the wrestling' is a defensible rendering of τῶν παλαισμάτων τὴν ὑπόθεσιν.

last_rejected.why: ἀπέκλεισας means 'closed' or 'barred,' not 'shut up'; and the metaphor is that the devil closed the arena/stadium, stopping the contest
last_rejected.ruling: ἀπέκλεισας means 'shut/closed'; 'shut up the arena' is within normal range. No meaning changed.

last_rejected.quote: should order his opponent's hands to be cut off and then strike him
last_rejected.source_quote: κελεύσειεν ἐκκοπῆναι τοῦ ἀνταγωνιστοῦ τὰς χεῖρας, καὶ οὕτως αὐτὸν παίοι
last_rejected.why: The subject is unclear: the beaten fighter orders his opponent's hands cut off so he can then strike him? Actually the grammar suggests the one receiving blows orders the cutting so that he (the opponent) can strike him? The Greek is compressed but 'οὕτως αὐτὸν παίοι' = 'and so he (the opponent with cut hands) would strike him'—the logic is paradoxical. English obscures this.
last_rejected.fix: should order his opponent's hands cut off—and so be struck by him
last_rejected.ruling: English correctly conveys the compressed Greek: the fighter orders opponent's hands cut, then strikes him. Logic is paradoxical but preserved.

last_rejected.quote: he breathed against it with all his force
last_rejected.why: ἔπνευσεν means 'breathed' but idiomatically 'directed his fury/attack'; 'ὅλος' means 'wholly,' not 'with all his force'—he became wholly focused on it, making himself more shameful
last_rejected.fix: he directed his whole fury against it
last_rejected.ruling: ὅλος adverbially = 'wholly/entirely'; 'with all his force' is a reasonable rendering of ὅλος modifying ἔπνευσεν. No meaning lost.

last_rejected.why: ὑπόκειται means 'lies beneath' or 'underlies,' not 'remains'; the nature of bodies is still there as substrate
last_rejected.fix: For there the nature of bodies underlies; only the composition is dissolved
last_rejected.ruling: ὑπόκειται means 'lies under/remains as substrate'; 'remains' captures the sense adequately. Mere preference.

last_rejected.quote: the very ground of the voice was destroyed
last_rejected.source_quote: αὐτὴ ἡ ὑπόθεσις τῆς φωνῆς ἀνῄρητο
last_rejected.why: Same word as earlier: ὑπόθεσις means 'foundation' or 'basis,' not 'ground' in the sense of reason/cause; here 'the very basis/substrate of voice'
last_rejected.fix: the very basis of the voice was destroyed
last_rejected.ruling: ὑπόθεσις means 'foundation/basis'; 'ground' is a valid English equivalent. No reader misled.

last_rejected.quote: the instrument lies useless from then on
last_rejected.why: κεῖται means 'lies' as in 'is situated/left,' but λοιπὸν = 'for the rest,' 'thereafter'; 'from then on' is okay but 'lies useless thereafter' is closer
last_rejected.ruling: λοιπὸν = 'thereafter/for the rest'; 'from then on' is equivalent. Mere preference, not an error.

last_rejected.why: ἐκπλήξεως is 'amazement' or 'wonder' experienced by hearers, not the song's quality; 'with greater wonder' or 'to greater amazement'
last_rejected.ruling: ἐκπλήξεως = 'astonishment/wonder'; 'with greater astonishment' is accurate. No meaning changed.
